bullets: The direction is called Search First and the search box is not the hero. The headline promises "in one search box" and then the actual field turns up below the fold as a 275px ghost pill inside the Product 01 pane, occupying about a third of the pane width and out-shouted by the black Search button sitting next to it, which is the darkest object in the upper half of the page. I would put the field in the hero at full measure, around 64px tall with the placeholder set in Inter Tight at body size, and drop the button to a quiet enter hint so the box is the thing you see, not its submit control.

The chip to page mechanic in the knowledge base pane is the best piece of product depiction across the whole set. Clicking "Refraction: collect or bill" opens a real situation page with its own Schibsted cap label, its answer in plain prose and its two flags, so the page demonstrates the product instead of describing it. It also shows up the two panes underneath it, where STEP 01 through STEP 04 and DAY 0 through DAY 42 are flowcharts of software rather than software, and the ops column then dies about 180px short of the ReExam column, leaving the pair looking unfinished at the bottom.

The sai-flag rows are bullet points wearing a costume, and the client asked for fewer bullets. There are five terracotta tick bars in the knowledge base pane alone, three more under the ops path, two in every situation page, and once you add the eyebrow discs, the timeline pearls and the callout corner brackets, the accent has stopped being punctuation and become texture. I would cut the trailing three flags under the KB pane entirely, keep the two inside the open situation page because they belong to it, and while you are in there mark the "This is where we would start you" pricing row so the recommendation is not hiding mid sentence in a table cell.
21.verdict: Best single interaction in the set and a genuinely quiet pricing table, but the weakest at delivering its own premise, so it is right for a client who will actually type into the box during a live demo rather than one skimming on their phone.

bullets: The three consoles genuinely work, and the ReExam one is the best single piece of explanation in the whole set. Six day markers down a spine, Day 10 pulled into terracotta with the TCPA chip sitting right underneath it, and I understand the compliance rule without reading a bullet about it. All three panels share the same skeleton (port label, title, control row, live status line, the picture, chip row, quiet price note) so the rhythm holds even though the three pictures are completely different shapes, which is exactly what the direction promised.

The sai-stamp corner brackets are broken and they are on every section, so the flaw compounds. Look at the questions list: six rows where LOOKUP, DATA · REEXAM, SYSTEMS all end at a different x, with the top-left bracket riding above the cap line and the bottom-right hanging into the row below. I would set the stamps in a right-aligned column at a fixed x, drop the bracket ticks entirely or lock them to the stamp's own box, and while I am in there replace the native ▶ disclosure triangles and the OS select chevrons in Console 03 with drawn ones, because borrowed browser chrome is the one thing that stops a page arguing 'this is real software'.

The bottom third undoes the discipline of the top. Section 04 Proof is six sentences in a table costume with a Detail column header doing no work at all, which is the ten-bullets habit the client asked you to kill, and Pricing is headed 'Stated plainly, stated once' when the same figures have already appeared three times in the console price notes above. Cut Proof to two or three numbers set as real figures, and either strip the per-console price lines or rename the pricing section honestly; also fix the testimonial grid, where the third card leaves a dead quarter of the page bottom-right and card two has a visible void under its attribution.
22.verdict: Strongest of the ten on product depiction and the only one where the interactive panels really carry the argument, but the stamp misalignment and a padded, repetitive bottom third keep it from being finished work.

bullets: The switch is the entire idea and it is parked in a static section 400px down, then never seen again across five thousand pixels of scroll. Worse, it defaults to "A desk on memory", so the rendered page is four grey key-value tables of the problem and almost none of the product. Pin the two chips into the dock as a sticky segmented control so the state travels with the reader, and default to "A desk on the system" so the software is what lands first.

The night proof block is the strongest moment on the page and the only place the eye genuinely stops on the way down. 76 / 4 / 0 set in Schibsted does more explaining than the eight rows of "The shelf" and "The caller on hold" above it combined, and the 0 is the argument. Pricing shows the same discipline: a bare table, terracotta on the setup numerals only, no pane and no CTA hanging off it, though the gap under "Plainly, and once." is tighter than every other title on the page and needs another step of air.

The ReExam section undoes the brief with seven status chips in a row, Live in, Contract, Patient data, Roles, Guarantee gate, Below the gate, Clock. That is ten bullets a section wearing chip clothing, and the mint and amber tints bring a second and third accent into a page that is supposed to run on terracotta alone. Keep three in neutral chips and push the rest into the questions list, and while you are there strip the pane off that questions section, the numbered rows are exactly right but the client asked for a list, not another card.
24.verdict: The sharpest single concept in the set, and the only one whose page is half invisible until someone clicks, so it reads mid-pack on the render and top three the moment the switch moves into the dock.

bullets: Section 03, the operations path, is the best thing on this page and the only place the design genuinely explains instead of describing. Step 02 forking into two named branches, with the outcome written inside each branch and the gap called out by name, is a mechanism I can read in three seconds without a bullet list. I would take that component's logic back into section 01 and let it carry more of the page.

The sequence in section 01 is stated twice and it costs the whole opening. The chip row already spells out Day 0 SMS, Day 3 Email, Day 10 Email only, Day 17 SMS, Day 28 SMS, Day 42 Email, and then the track directly beneath repeats the same six days with the same modality words, so the eye reads the same list back to back and the Day 42 chip orphans onto its own row. Kill the chip row entirely, make the track rows themselves the click target, and let the three answer states be the only control in the section.

The knowledge base search box is the weakest craft detail: it is styled as a ghost pill at the same height and roughly the same width as the six result pills stacked right under it, with no field inset and no magnifier, so it reads as a seventh disabled chip rather than the search box the entire section is built around. Give it a real field treatment, full measure, white ground, and a visible caret, and add a rule or a gap before the results so the input and its output are not the same object. The pricing footnote has the same slackness in content form: the heading promises "Plainly, once" and then four sentences dump five more numbers on me, so trim it to the tier recommendation and move the rest to the call.
23.verdict: Upper third of the set on structure and the strongest argument for ReExam as a product, but it repeats itself where the others cut, so it is right for an owner who wants to see the actual run rather than a browser skimming.

bullets: The search field in the knowledge base tab is the one control the whole page is built around and it is a raw browser input: a hairline box about 34 characters wide, grey placeholder, with a plain body-copy label sitting above it. Next to the frosted panes and the pill tab row it looks like a form someone forgot to style. Give it real height, the pane's frosted fill and a terracotta focus ring, drop the label and let the placeholder carry it, and kill one of the two headings stacked three lines apart above it.

The one window, three tabs premise is the best structural idea in the set and it is why this page is short. You commit the entire product story to a single pane instead of three stacked sections, so the eye never leaves that frame, and the four decision chips plus the ReExam day track mean a visitor is operating the thing rather than reading about it. The Questions section is exactly the brief too, a compact click to open list with no card, it just sits in a pane about twice the width the list needs, so trim the pane or let the list run the full measure.

The client asked for fewer bullets and got table rows instead. Five two column tables on one page, and every tab lands in one, so everything below the demo reads as flat grey text in columns. The Proof table is the worst of it: 27, 76, 4 and 0 are the strongest content you have and they are set at body size in a narrow left column, so pull them out as a Schibsted display row with the label underneath and let the counts actually count.
25.verdict: The sharpest concept of the ten and the only one a prospect actually uses before the call, held back by unfinished typographic craft inside the widget itself.

bullets: Section 01 is the best product depiction in this whole set. A real search field that types "refraction" for you, a live count line that says "1 page matches", and an open decision lookup with actual desk answers underneath is software behaving, not a diagram of software. One fix: the input is styled as sai-btn ghost so it sits next to "Show all" as a second pill and nobody will read it as a field. Give it an inset well, a caret, a wider measure, and let it stop pretending to be a button.

The reveal mechanic is eating the two sections it exists to explain. In the full page render ReExam says "0 of 6 touches sent" over an empty spine and Operations says "0 of 4 steps" over nothing at all, so a third of the page is a headline, two controls and white space. I would make the resting state carry content already, say day 0 and day 3 drawn plus STEP 01 filed, and animate the remainder in from there. Nothing should ever paint to zero, because a screenshot, a print, a fast scroll and a dead script all land on the same empty frame.

The client asked for fewer bullets and this page mostly moved them into tables and pills instead of into pictures. Five tables run down the page (build spec, guarantee terms, proof, founders, pricing) and the green BAA, Alongside, Rules, Report chips are a second accent colour doing claims work that the guarantee table already does. Drop the green to the neutral glass treatment so terracotta stays the only accent, and cut the second testimonial: "Thank you for all of your help on this project" is a pleasantry occupying a full card next to a genuinely useful quote about adoption habits.
26.verdict: Strongest product depiction of the ten and the only one where the software actually behaves, but the empty resting state makes it the most fragile: right for a live demo, wrong for anyone who skims or screenshots it.

bullets: The hero is the best idea in the set: "Your practice runs on 5 parts. We built 3 of them" plus a diagram where terracotta outline and crop marks mean "this one is ours and it opens below". That is the accent carrying meaning rather than decorating, and it explains the offer with no bullets at all. Two fixes: the SVG is centred inside a full width figure while the h1 sits flush left, so there is a dead half column under "Your practice", and the edge words (calls, replies, books, time off) float well clear of the lines they name. Left align the drawing to the type, let it get bigger, and set each label on its own line with a small knockout so the reader never has to guess which arrow it belongs to.

The spec tables are where the brief quietly gets ignored. ReExam's "The terms" table is eleven rows of prose, three of them about the guarantee (the quote, the gate, the clock), and the knowledge base and proof tables run eight and six more. A table row holding twenty five words of copy is a bullet in a costume, so keep four rows visible per product and push the rest behind a "the terms in full" disclosure, which is a pattern this page already owns.

The questions section nails what was asked for, a six row click to open list with no card around it, and pricing sits as a quiet table under "Plainly, once" without shouting. Two things drag on it: the left rail categories are doing no work ("Who" next to "Who is actually doing the work?", "Fixes" next to "Who fixes it when a page is wrong?"), and the pearl discs on that rail are dot-pills the system says no to, with "Insurance" and "Contract" running straight into them. Drop the rail from the questions block entirely and replace the raw browser triangles with a styled marker.
27.verdict: Strongest hero concept of the ten and the only one where the accent is genuinely a legend, but the heaviest body in the set, so it suits the buyer who wants to poke at three working widgets rather than the one skimming on a phone.

bullets: The pricing section is the best argument in the whole set for this direction. "Every price, in one table" with hairline rows, small caps column heads and no tier cards, no badges, no most-popular flag, means the money reads as reference material rather than a pitch, and the per section one liners like "Price: $2,500 setup, then $299 a month" set in small grey type do exactly what the client asked for. Terracotta is disciplined too: the hero em, the eyebrows, the DAY 10 entry and the night close, nothing else.

The questions section is raw browser furniture and it is the one thing the client specifically called out. The six sai-faq details render with the native black disclosure triangle, the summaries are bold at lede size so they visually outrank the H2 "The six we always get." above them, and there is no rule between rows so the list reads as six floating bold sentences. I would style it properly: hairline between each row, question at body size weight 500 with the accent used only on a small chevron that rotates on open, and let the H2 win the top of the block.

Every section ends in the same ladder of grey hairline footnotes, and the strongest fact on the page dies in one of them. "60 to 100 admin hours a year" sits at body size in a note stacked directly above "Price: included in tier 3", so the number and the price read at identical weight. Promote that figure to a real stat line in Schibsted numerals, and cut the two "How it sits on the desk" tables down to a caption, because five near identical tables by the time I reach pricing is prose wearing a grid, the opposite of the DAY 10 rule flag which is the one place this page genuinely explains without words.
28.verdict: Best pricing treatment of the ten and the only page where price truly reads as a footnote, but at 7,600px with five explainer tables it is a long page in quiet clothing rather than a quiet page, so it lands upper middle for a client who asked for less.

bullets: The gate is the best idea in the set and it actually works as design rather than as a claim. "The guarantee starts at 1,000. Below 500 we say no." sits at the top, three branch cards under Step 02 name exactly what you would be offered in each band, and the verdict chip changes with your own number, so the page disqualifies people without a paragraph of hedging. The Day 10 TCPA warn chip in the night window does the same trick, explaining a legal rule in five words where every other version of this page would have written three sentences.

The one thing you need the visitor to do is typing their count, and you have dressed that input as the third of four identical white pills next to Lower 100, Raise 100 and Clear. Nothing signals it is a field except grey placeholder text, so the whole widget can be walked past. Make the number the object: a large Schibsted numeral field with a terracotta underline and caret, with Lower and Raise reduced to small quiet steppers beside it. While you are in there, rescale the gauge, because at a 2,000 ceiling the gate sits at the halfway mark and the entire right half of the track carries no meaning.

The knowledge base section is where you quietly put the ten bullets back. Every one of the eight pages is three bold-led bullets plus a paragraph that starts with the bold word "Exception.", and reading two in a row you feel the template rather than the answer. Show one page in full, let the other seven open as a title and a single decisive line, and cut the second testimonial entirely, because "Thank you for all of your help on this project" earns no space and it undercuts your own header about including the one that is not praise.
29.verdict: Strongest concept of the ten and the only one that lets a visitor rule themselves out, but the longest and most template-bound execution, so it is right for the owner who wants to check the gate before they book and wrong for anyone skimming.

bullets: The night deck is the best product depiction in the round. A bare hero with no pane, then the only dark region on the page arrives exactly where I am meant to look, and putting the lit cream day sheet inside it makes the search field read as a screen rather than a diagram of one. Two things I would fix inside it: the mint LOOKUP chip is the only green on the page and it says nothing on its own because the detail text never shows, so cut it, and trim the roughly 150px of dead sheet under the exception callout so the window closes on the content.

The questions section is still a card, which is the one thing the client asked it not to be, and each row carries two markers at once: the house sphere bullet from sai-bullets plus the browser default black triangle from the details summary. That black triangle belongs to no design system. Drop the pane, drop the ul, and make it six hairline separated rows with a terracotta chevron or plus that rotates on open.

In ReExam the three bullets for exam type intervals, contact lens runout and family batching sit flush under DAY 42 with no separation and at a different left edge from the timeline entries, so they read as a broken seventh touch. That trailing bullet list also undercuts the premise: I just stepped through six touches and then got told three more things in prose. Either fold those rules into the timeline as conditions on the rail or give them their own caps label and a rule above them.
30.verdict: The strongest product depiction of the ten because of the single night window, held back from being the outright best page by a questions section that ignores the brief and a ReExam tail that reverts to bullets; right for the buyer who wants to touch the thing before the call.
